title: Who Else Is There Besides Me?
hook: Shumbha says the goddess fights with borrowed strength; she answers that she is alone, and all the goddesses go back into her
carry: the many goddesses are one devi
tomorrow: back in the forest, the goddess asks two men what they want. what do they ask?

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Raktabija multiplied with every drop of blood, until Kali caught each one.

It's an old insult: you didn't really do it; somebody did it for you. In the ninth chapter the younger brother, Nishumbha, falls. Even then, another figure rises out of his chest shouting stop, and the goddess laughs and cuts off its head. Now only Shumbha is left, his brother dead, his army gone. In the tenth chapter he looks across at the goddess, surrounded by Kali and the other goddesses, and throws the insult. In paraphrase: don't be so proud, Durga. You fight leaning on the strength of others.
screen: `NISHUMBHA FALLS.` → `ONLY SHUMBHA IS LEFT.` → `YOU FIGHT WITH OTHERS' STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: The goddess answers, in paraphrase: I am alone here in the world. Who else is there besides me? Look, you fool: these are my own powers, going back into me. And they do. Brahmani on her swan, the goddess of Shiva's trident, the goddess on Garuda, the boar-faced one, the lion-faced one: the text says they all enter her body. The field is suddenly empty but for two: Shumbha, and Ambika, alone. All along she has seemed to have helpers: Kali from her brow, goddesses from the gods' bodies, troops from her breath. Shumbha took them for outside help. Her answer is that there never was anyone else; in her words, every one was her own power, in another form. Then the last fight. They battle with every weapon, then bare hands. Shumbha seizes her and leaps into the sky, and they fight in the air with nothing to stand on. At last she whirls him around and throws him down, and as he rushes at her one last time she pierces his chest with her spear. He falls, and the text describes the whole world going calm. The rivers run in their courses again, the winds blow gently, the sun shines clear. Shakta teachers cite her line for one of their central teachings: Durga, Kali, the Mothers, all are forms of one Devi, the great goddess. Many Hindus say the same of God: one, worshiped in many forms. It's how a family altar can hold several images and still pray to one.
screen: `I AM ALONE HERE IN THE WORLD.` · `THE GODDESSES GO BACK INTO HER.` · `THE MANY WERE ALWAYS ONE.` · `A FIGHT IN THE SKY, THEN STILLNESS.` · then, large: `WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?`

segments.voice: If your family keeps an altar, or you know one, bring its images to mind one at a time, whoever is there, and give each a breath. Then let them gather into one, the way the goddesses walked back into her, and rest there. If you pray, speak to that one in your own words; if not, let the stillness after the battle be enough, the breath running in its own course, the way the rivers did.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the two brothers fall, and the goddess answers: I am alone here in the world; who else is there besides me?
Your line: the many goddesses are one Devi. The helpers were her own powers all along. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Sanskrit: ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra, 'I am alone here in the world,' the goddess's answer to Shumbha.

notes: Chapters 9 and 10 paraphrased. Ch. 9: Nishumbha struck down; from his heart another figure emerges crying 'stop!'; the goddess laughs and cuts off its head. Ch. 10: Shumbha's taunt (balāvalepād duṣṭe tvaṃ mā durge garvam āvaha / anyāsāṃ balam āśritya yuddhyase): her answer ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra dvitīyā kā mamāparā / paśyaitā duṣṭa mayy eva viśantyo madvibhūtayaḥ; the goddesses enter her body and Ambika alone remains; the fight in the sky; she throws him down and pierces him with her spear; nature becomes calm. Confirm.
The goddess is addressed as 'Durga' in Shumbha's taunt; confirm the name in that verse.
Two readings of the line are attributed to teachers without ranking; confirm they are fair.
Devanagari for ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra (एकैवाहं जगत्यत्र) and the pronunciation: confirm.
The goddesses are named generically (Brahmani, the boar-faced, the lion-faced); 'the goddess of Shiva's trident' stands for Maheshvari. Confirm.
